paras: The threatened lynching of William Nichols occurred on August 4, 1903, when about 200 people at the depot in Belle Centre, Ohio, called for Nichols, a Black prisoner accused of murder, to be shot or hanged as his train passed on the way to the Kenton jail. The train pulled out, a second crowd threatened him at Kenton, and the sheriff lodged him in jail unharmed. Papers across the country ran it as a lynching avoided; Nichols was electrocuted for the murder in December 1904.

Nichols, described as "colored," "a negro" and "a mulatto," lived with Minard, an elderly Civil War veteran, near McGuffey in Hardin County. Minard disappeared on Tuesday, July 28, and on August 1 neighbors found his decomposed body beside the Erie Railroad near McGuffey. According to his sister, Nichols told her he had killed Minard, and the Bellefontaine Republican reported he showed her $136 and a watch. A Kenton wire report said a posse was pursuing him and that "there are threats that if captured he will be lynched."

Sheriff Griffith of Hardin County arrested Nichols at Carmel and brought him by train toward Kenton. When the train reached Belle Centre, about 200 residents of the vicinity where Minard had lived were waiting at the depot. Once Nichols was seen in the car, the crowd raised cries of "shoot him" and "hang him," and, "fearing mob violence," the train quickly pulled out.

Another crowd met the train at Kenton and made "many angry threats," but the sheriff took his prisoner to the jail without trouble. Nichols denied his guilt, though the dispatch said he had made "many conflicting statements."

A week later the Bellefontaine Republican reported that he blamed two nephews and asked why he had not informed on them at the time. The grand jury at Kenton indicted him for first-degree murder in September 1903, and in November Judge Lemert sentenced him to be electrocuted on February 13.

He was electrocuted at the Ohio penitentiary in December 1904, aged 68. The Bellefontaine Republican called him a Union army veteran and printed his confession that he killed Minard in self-defense during a drunken gambling quarrel. No report of any action against members of the crowds at Belle Centre or Kenton was found.

All accounts of the crowds came from one Associated Press dispatch from Kenton, which ran on August 5 in the Richmond Times Dispatch as "Negro Carried Through Angry Mob," in the Savannah Morning News as "Mob Bent on Lynching Met at Train," and in the New-York Tribune as "Ohio Crowds Threaten Negro." Later copies included the Raleigh News & Observer's "Ohio Mobs Outwitted" on August 6 and the Mitchell Capital's "Would Lynch Negro," subheaded "Ohio Negro Dodges the Rope and Is Safe in Jail."

The Indianapolis Journal's shortened "Threats, but No Lynching" mentioned only the Kenton crowd, and the Little Falls Herald printed one sentence. The New York Herald ran it as "Train Saves a Prisoner" among other mob reports, and the Kenosha Telegraph-Courier said the officers "were equal to the occasion." None criticized the crowds, and headlines such as "Negro Murderer Caught" and "Slayer of Alpha Minard" treated Nichols as the killer.

The local Bellefontaine Republican followed the case to the execution, calling Nichols "colored (nearly white)," but its items found do not mention the crowds. All coverage found came from white papers; no Black-press report of the episode was found.

The murdered man's first name appears as Harry in the first wire, Alpha in the Associated Press dispatch, and Alfred in the 1904 execution reports, while the local paper first printed him as "A. Minor." Accounts of the death differ: a bullet in the breast at his home (first wire), a body by the railroad shot in the cheek (local paper), or a stone and two shots (confession).

bases: Crowds at the Belle Centre depot and at Kenton shouted for a prisoner accused of murder to be shot or hanged, but he reached jail unharmed, a threatened lynching (A9, A11, A10).

A crowd of about 200 with no lawful authority called for Nichols, accused of murdering Minard, to be shot or hanged, but no one was killed; he was later executed by the state after indictment and sentence (A11, A22, A26).

Every report of the depot and Kenton crowds traces to one Associated Press dispatch from Kenton (A8, A11, A12); the murder accusation and the earlier lynching threats are reported independently by a wire (A1), a Bellefontaine special (A2) and the local paper (A6).

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal short version
accounts.gist: Only a crowd at Kenton made angry threats; the crowd did not molest the prisoner.

accounts.label: Sister's account (via wire and local paper)
accounts.gist: Nichols told his sister he had killed Minard; versions say he took $200 or showed her $136 and a watch, saying he won the money at poker and killed the man in a quarrel.

accounts.label: Nichols's own statements
accounts.gist: He first denied guilt, then blamed two nephews, and in a confession before execution said he killed Minard in self-defense in a drunken gambling quarrel.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the AP dispatch verbatim under headlines such as 'Ohio Crowds Threaten Negro' and 'Negro Carried Through Angry Mob', with no comment on the crowds.
Headlines presented Nichols as guilty ('Slayer of Alpha Minard', 'Negro Murderer Caught') and the escape as a near-miss ('Ohio Negro Dodges the Rope and Is Safe in Jail').
The Kenosha Telegraph-Courier paired it with an Idaho case as 'Mob All Along the Line' and credited the officers, who 'were equal to the occasion.'
The local Bellefontaine Republican followed the murder case and execution in detail and editorially doubted Nichols's claim that his nephews did it; its items found do not mention the depot crowd.

conflicts.note: The local paper uses 'A. Minor' in August 1903 and 'A. Minard' later (A22); no version is clearly better.
A10 is a shortened copy of the same dispatch, so the omission is an abridgment rather than a denial.
